name: Ahilud
title: Father of Jehoshaphat, the royal administrator
summary: Ahilud is mentioned indirectly in the biblical texts through two of his sons, both of whom held central positions in the administration of the united kingdom of Israel. His son Jehoshaphat served as royal chancellor (Hebrew: mazkir, 'the one who reminds/recalls') under King David and continued in this role under King Solomon—a position that entailed responsibility for royal annals and communication between the court and the people. The other son, Baana, was appointed as one of Solomon's twelve district governors and administered a strategically important region around Taanach and Megiddo. That two sons from the same family served in the national administration under two kings points to an influential family with strong roots in Jerusalem's royal power structure.
roles: Part of the court's circle of influence

versions.summary: Ahilud is known from the biblical texts exclusively through his sons, who both held prominent positions in the administration of the united Israelite kingdom. His son Jehoshaphat served as royal chancellor (Hebrew: mazkir) under both King David and King Solomon, while his son Baana was one of Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for the area around Taanach and Megiddo. The family's presence in the royal administration throughout two kings' reigns testifies that they belonged to an influential lineage with close ties to the royal court in Jerusalem.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word 'mazkir' (מזכיר), translated as 'royal chancellor' or 'historian', comes from the root z-k-r meaning 'to remember'. The title likely refers to someone responsible for keeping royal annals and serving as a kind of communications minister between the king and the people.

The name Ahilud (אֲחִילוּד) may mean 'brother of one who is born' or 'my brother is born', composed of the Hebrew elements 'ach' (brother) and 'yalad' (to bear). This is a typical Semitic personal name from the Israelite monarchy period.

The administration of David and Solomon, as described in 2 Sam 8:16–18 and 1 Kgs 4:1–19, shows similarities to Egyptian and Mesopotamian bureaucratic structures. The fact that Ahilud's sons held central roles under two successive kings suggests that offices were somewhat hereditary in the administration of the united kingdom.

Solomon's division of the kingdom into twelve administrative districts (1 Kgs 4:7–19), where Baana son of Ahilud governed the district around Taanach and Megiddo, is of archaeological interest. Excavations at Megiddo have uncovered administrative buildings from the tenth century BCE that may be linked to this administrative structure.

In the royal administration of the united kingdom, the royal chancellor (mazkir) likely served as a link between the king and the people. The position can be compared with the Egyptian title 'whm.w' (herald), reflecting the strong Egyptian influence on the state apparatus in Israel during the time of David and Solomon.

In rabbinic tradition, the role of mazkir has been understood as more than a mere chronicler. The role likely also included advisory functions and access to the king's inner circle, making it probable that Ahilud himself was a man with considerable social and political influence.
